topic.title: The IMAX seat is the film's real product
topic.claim: Ramayana's IMAX shows sell out first because people are paying for a story they can tell afterwards, not for a better film.
topic.behaviour: Audiences skip the regular screen and book the biggest screen for a big film, even at a higher ticket price. They post the seat or the screen, not the scenes.
topic.mechanism: A large film gets sold as an event, and an event needs a visible badge. IMAX is the badge, and the multiplex gets more per seat.
topic.group: Urban 24 to 32 year olds who book the 'right' screen for big releases
topic.moment: You open the booking app for a big film and your thumb goes straight to the IMAX show, even though the regular show is half empty.

turn.believed: People pay more for IMAX because the film looks better on it.
turn.actually: People pay more because the screen announces that they were there at the big moment.

topic.because: The cinema earns more per seat, and the film earns a bigger opening. You get something to post, so everybody is happy except your wallet.

proof.fact: IMAX is about 25% of Ramayana's advance collections from 3.8% of screenings, averaging about 170 tickets per show against 35 for regular shows.

topic.payoff: Test: would you still pick that screen if you could not tell anyone which one you sat in?
topic.send_to: The friend who books the premium show for every big release and calls it 'worth it'.
real_details: Premium recliner seats sold out in some Mumbai cinemas.
topic.news_peg: Ramayana: Part 1 advance booking numbers reported 26 October 2026, release 5 November.
topic.why_now: The film opens next week and the screen choice is being made right now.

score.why: People pay for the screen that says they were there. Reads as status, not a film review.

sources.fact: About ten days before release, IMAX shows of Ramayana: Part 1 were selling about 400% faster than regular shows, at an average ticket price of Rs 1,095 against about Rs 380 for regular shows.
sources.excerpt: while regular shows are averaging around Rs 380 per ticket, IMAX is clocking an average price of Rs 1,095. ... the sharpest push is coming from IMAX, where shows are selling at a pace nearly 400 percent higher than regular screenings. ... IMAX screenings have sold over 23,000 tickets across 140 shows, averaging about 170 tickets per screening.

sources.fact: By 29 October 2026, Ramayana: Part 1 had sold around 3.07 lakh advance tickets and collected Rs 15.94 crore including block seats. Premium formats, including IMAX, supplied about 27% of the gross from a small share of shows.
sources.excerpt: contributed around 27 pc of the gross ... around 3.07 lakh advance tickets across the country. ... collected Rs 15.94 crore in advance bookings across India ... Excluding block seats, the gross is Rs 13.12 crore.

cover.headline: Ramayana's IMAX shows fill first because you're buying [a story to tell]
cover.sub: Same film on every screen. Only one ends up on your story.

paragraphs: Ramayana's IMAX shows fill first because you're buying a story to tell.
slides.why_swipe: If it isn't the picture, what am I paying for?

paragraphs: The group chat has been at it since the trailer dropped. Someone finally types "book karo" and you open the app.
Same evening, two shows. The regular one still has the good middle rows open. Your thumb is on IMAX before you've even looked at them.
slides.why_swipe: Why skip the easy seats for the pricier show?

paragraphs: That IMAX seat costs about ₹700 more. You tell yourself a film this big deserves the big screen.
And some of that is true. The screen is taller, and the sound lands in your chest during the big scenes.
slides.why_swipe: So where does the real reason show up?

paragraphs: But watch your phone that night. Before the lights go down, the ticket goes on your story, IMAX logo carefully in frame.
A week later someone at work asks how the film was. **"We saw it in IMAX" comes out before a single scene does.**
The cinema earns more on every seat. The film gets a bigger opening to announce. You get proof you were there for the big moment.
**That story is the cinema's ad, and you paid the extra to run it.**
slides.why_swipe: So what would I pick if nobody could see it?

paragraphs: Now imagine the ticket just said "Screen 4". No logo, nothing worth a photo, nobody ever finding out which seat you took.
Suddenly that regular show with the open middle rows looks fine. **Would you still pick IMAX if you couldn't tell anyone you sat there?**

end.save: Open it again the next time your thumb hovers over the IMAX show.
end.send: Send it to the friend who books the premium show for every big release and calls it 'worth it'.
end.promise: Why we pay what we pay.

draft.caption: The IMAX logo on your story got more careful framing than anything in the film.
draft.alt_text: Carousel about Ramayana: Part 1 IMAX bookings. The cover says IMAX shows fill first because you're buying a story to tell, not a better film. The slides follow a reader whose group chat says 'book karo'. They open a booking app and pick the IMAX show without looking at the regular show, which still has good middle rows open. The IMAX seat costs about ₹700 more, and the reader admits the bigger screen and sound are real. Then they post the ticket with the IMAX logo in frame, and when asked about the film they mention the screen before any scene. The cinema earns more per seat, the film gets a bigger opening, and the reader gets proof they were there, so their story becomes the cinema's ad that they paid extra to run. It ends with a test: if the ticket only said 'Screen 4' and nobody could know, the regular show suddenly looks fine. Would you still pick IMAX if you couldn't tell anyone?

claims.text: An IMAX ticket for Ramayana: Part 1 costs about ₹700 more than a regular ticket on average.
claims.derived_from: ₹1,095 average IMAX ticket minus ₹380 average regular ticket = ₹715, rounded to about ₹700

claims.text: Ramayana's IMAX shows are filling faster than regular shows.
